headline: Documentary About Theranos Founder Becomes a Box Office Hit

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A new movie called a documentary has made a lot of money. A documentary is a movie that tells a true story instead of a made-up one. This one is about a woman named Elizabeth Holmes, who started a company that got into trouble for lying about what it could do. The movie is called "You Can See Everything." It was made by two filmmakers, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. So far, people around the world have paid more than $100 million to watch it in theaters! Most of that money came from people in the United States. The movie cost only $7 million to make, so making over $100 million is a huge success. Soon, the movie will open in more countries, like Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina. If it keeps doing well, it could become one of the most successful documentaries ever made, even beating famous ones like "March of the Penguins" and "Fahrenheit 9/11." People are even wondering if it might win awards, like an Oscar!

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: A documentary film has become a huge money-making success, earning more than $100 million worldwide. The movie, called "You Can See Everything," was made by filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim and tells the true story of Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of a company called Theranos that was accused of lying about its medical technology. Most of the movie's earnings, about $93 million, came from audiences in the United States. This is a big deal because documentaries usually don't make as much money as big action movies or superhero films. The movie was made for only $7 million, which means the studio that released it, A24, earned way more money than it spent — a huge financial win. The film is about to open in more countries, including Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina, so its total earnings could grow even more. If it keeps making money, it might beat the two highest-earning documentaries of all time: "March of the Penguins," which made $127 million, and "Fahrenheit 9/11," which made $222 million. People are now wondering if the movie might also get nominated for awards, like the Oscars, since it has become such a surprising hit both with audiences and at the box office.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: A documentary film has achieved something rare in the movie industry — earning more than $100 million worldwide. The film, titled "You Can See Everything," was created by filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim and focuses on the true story of Elizabeth Holmes, who founded a company called Theranos. Theranos claimed to have invented groundbreaking blood-testing technology, but it was later revealed that much of what the company promised was false, leading to a major scandal. This documentary explores that story, and audiences have responded strongly: the film has earned $102.4 million so far, with the vast majority — about $93.4 million — coming from viewers in the United States. What makes this especially impressive is that the film was made for a relatively small budget of just $7 million. For an independent studio like A24, known for producing creative, lower-budget films rather than big blockbusters, this kind of financial success is extraordinary. The movie is set to expand into new international markets soon, including Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina, which means its total earnings will likely keep climbing. If that happens, it could surpass the two highest-grossing documentaries in history: "March of the Penguins," which earned $127 million, and "Fahrenheit 9/11," which made $222 million. This success matters because documentaries typically attract smaller audiences than fictional dramas or action movies, so a true story about a corporate scandal pulling in blockbuster-level numbers is unusual. It suggests that audiences are hungry for real-life stories, especially ones involving deception, ambition, and consequences. There's also growing buzz that the film could receive award nominations, including possibly an Oscar, which would add even more recognition to its commercial success.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: A documentary titled "You Can See Everything," directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, has crossed a major milestone by earning more than $100 million at the global box office — a feat accomplished by very few nonfiction films in cinema history. The documentary examines the story of Elizabeth Holmes, founder of the now-infamous company Theranos, which claimed to have revolutionized blood testing before investigations revealed that its technology didn't work as promised. This scandal became one of the most notable examples of corporate fraud in recent memory, and the documentary's exploration of it has clearly resonated with audiences. Of the film's $102.4 million total earnings, the overwhelming majority — roughly $93.4 million — has come from U.S. moviegoers, though that is expected to change soon. The film is scheduled to open in several additional countries, including Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina, in late November, which should push its worldwide total even higher. What makes this success particularly notable is the film's modest production budget of about $7 million. For A24, the independent studio behind the film and known for favoring artistic, lower-budget projects over mainstream blockbusters, this represents an enormous return on investment. If international audiences continue to embrace the film, it stands a strong chance of overtaking the two documentaries that currently hold box office records: "March of the Penguins" at $127 million and "Fahrenheit 9/11" at $222 million. This kind of success raises interesting questions about audience appetite for real-world stories, particularly ones involving fraud, ambition, and accountability — themes that seem to captivate viewers across demographics. It also signals a potential shift in how studios view documentaries: rather than being a niche genre with limited commercial appeal, a well-marketed, well-reviewed documentary can now compete with — and even outperform — many scripted films. Beyond box office numbers, there's growing speculation that the film could earn awards recognition, including a possible Oscar nomination, which would further validate its impact. The playful suggestion that the film's reach might soon extend to "the International Space Station" underscores just how surprising and widespread its success has become.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: The documentary "You Can See Everything," directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, has reached a box office milestone achieved by only a handful of nonfiction films: surpassing $100 million in worldwide earnings. The film chronicles the rise and fall of Elizabeth Holmes, founder of Theranos, a company that promised to revolutionize medical diagnostics with technology that could supposedly run dozens of tests from a single drop of blood. That promise later collapsed under scrutiny, exposing widespread fraud and turning Holmes into a symbol of Silicon Valley overreach. The documentary's commercial performance suggests that this real-life story of ambition and deception continues to captivate the public years after the scandal first broke. Currently, the film has earned $102.4 million globally, with roughly $93.4 million of that coming from U.S. audiences — a disproportionate share that reflects both the story's American origins and its early, limited international release. That imbalance is expected to shift soon, as the film prepares to debut in Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina in late November, with additional countries likely to follow in the coming months. Each new market represents an opportunity for the film's total earnings to climb further, and industry analysts are watching closely to see whether it can challenge, or even dethrone, the two documentaries that currently hold box office records: "March of the Penguins," which earned $127 million worldwide, and "Fahrenheit 9/11," the politically charged film that grossed $222 million. What makes this financial success particularly striking is the economics behind it. The film was produced on a relatively modest budget of $7 million, meaning its box office haul represents a return on investment that few films, documentary or otherwise, ever achieve. For A24, the production company behind the film and a studio celebrated for backing artistically ambitious, lower-budget projects rather than conventional blockbusters, this outcome reinforces its reputation for identifying and cultivating unexpected hits. More broadly, the film's success invites reflection on shifting audience tastes. Documentaries have traditionally occupied a niche corner of the film industry, often praised critically but rarely achieving mainstream box office traction. A film about corporate fraud drawing blockbuster-level audiences suggests that viewers are increasingly drawn to stories that blend journalism, drama, and moral reckoning — particularly when the subject matter touches on themes of trust, technology, and accountability that feel relevant to contemporary life. There is also mounting speculation that the film could receive major awards recognition, potentially including an Oscar nomination, which would further cement its cultural and critical significance. Whether or not that happens, the film has already demonstrated that compelling true stories, when told with skill and marketed effectively, can compete commercially with much larger, fictional productions.

questions: Why do you think people are so interested in watching true stories about scandals and fraud, like the one at the center of this documentary?
If a company in your community made false promises about a product, like Theranos did, how do you think people should respond or hold that company accountable?
Do you think movies and documentaries can influence how people think about businesses or technology? Why or why not?
